subject: Accounting
title: Special Order Pricing
description: A 60-second lesson on Special Order Pricing.

hook.text: A hotel chain offers to buy 5,000 pillows at $8 each. Your normal price is $15. Accept or refuse?

buildup.text: Special order analysis asks: will this order contribute to profit, even at a lower price?

discovery.text: If the price exceeds variable cost and there's spare capacity, the order adds to profit.

twist.text: But if regular customers learn about the discount, they'll demand the same price—eroding margins.

climax.text: The decision depends on capacity, variable costs, and whether the deal stays confidential.

punchline.text: Below list price can still mean above zero profit.

quiz.question: When should a company accept a special order below normal price?
options: When the price exceeds variable cost and spare capacity exists

details.summary: Special order pricing evaluates whether to accept a one-time order at a price below the normal selling price. This topic explains the relevant cost analysis for special orders, including excess capacity, incremental costs, and potential risks.
details.whyItMatters: Rejecting a special order that covers its incremental costs leaves money on the table. Accepting one that doesn't—or that cannibalizes regular sales—destroys value. The analysis depends on understanding which costs are relevant.
takeaways: Accept a special order if the price exceeds the incremental cost and excess capacity exists
Fixed costs are usually irrelevant because they won't change from accepting the order
Consider qualitative risks: will the special price become the customer's expected price in future orders?

faq.question: How do you evaluate a special order at below-normal price?
faq.answer: Compare the special order price to the incremental (variable) cost per unit. If the order price exceeds incremental cost and there is unused capacity, the order contributes additional profit. Fixed costs are irrelevant since they're already being paid.

faq.question: What are the risks of accepting a special order?
faq.answer: Key risks include regular customers learning of the lower price and demanding similar deals, the special order becoming a recurring expectation, capacity constraints affecting regular production, and the order establishing a below-market price precedent in the industry.
